title: Derivatives, units and finite differences

objectives.text: Derive a derivative from its difference-quotient limit, track output/input units and distinguish local linear sensitivity from a finite scenario or a derivative at a kink.
Derive first/second-order finite-difference truncation errors and evaluate step-size tradeoffs with domain, representability and function-evaluation error checks.

blocks.markdown: For a real function f on an open neighborhood of x, f'(x)=lim_{h→0}(f(x+h)-f(x))/h when the two-sided finite limit exists. The numerator has output units and h has input units, so the derivative has output/input units. A price sensitivity per dollar is not the same numeric value as a sensitivity per cent. A derivative is a local limit, not a claim that one finite change equals derivative times change exactly.

blocks.title: Derive and use a local sensitivity

steps.text: For f(x)=x², expand (x+h)²-x²=2xh+h². For nonzero h, the quotient is 2x+h; as h→0 it tends to 2x.

If x is time in seconds and f(x)=3x² metres with coefficient 3 in metres/second², then f'(2)=6*2=12 metres/second. The coefficient carries units; writing just x² without its physical coefficient would hide them.

For a finite time increment h, the exact position change is 6xh+3h². The derivative-only estimate 6xh omits 3h². With x=2 and h=0.5 seconds, actual change 6.75 metres differs from linear estimate 6 metres.

If new coordinate u=100x expresses the same input in smaller units, g(u)=f(u/100). Difference quotients give g'(u)=f'(u/100)/100. Per-small-unit sensitivity changes; the represented physical change does not.

blocks.markdown: For several real coordinates, partial derivative ∂f/∂x_j varies coordinate j while holding the others fixed. Differentiability means f(x+δ)=f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀδ+o(||δ||). Then the derivative along direction d is ∇f(x)ᵀd. For f(x,y)=x²+3y², ∇f=(2x,6y); at (1,2), a small δ=(0.01,-0.02) has linear change 2*0.01+12*(-0.02)=-0.22. Each partial has its own output/coordinate units. Comparing gradient coordinates or taking a norm needs a chosen geometry/scaling. Existence of partials alone does not establish full differentiability.

At differentiability points, linear combinations differentiate termwise; the product rule is (fg)'=f'g+fg', and the chain rule for g(f(x)) is g'(f(x))*f'(x). These follow by adding/subtracting the appropriate cross term in difference quotients and taking limits. For example d[(x²+1)²]/dx=2(x²+1)*2x. This lesson uses small polynomial derivatives with independently expanded identities, not an automatic-differentiation engine or a full calculus course. More explicitly, (f(x+h)g(x+h)-f(x)g(x))/h = [(f(x+h)-f(x))/h]*g(x+h) + f(x)*[(g(x+h)-g(x))/h]. Differentiability implies continuity, giving the product rule in the limit. For the chain rule, put Δ=f(x+h)-f(x)=f'(x)h+o(h); the outer differentiability expansion gives g(f(x)+Δ)-g(f(x))=g'(f(x))*Δ+o(|Δ|). Since Δ=O(h), division by h gives the product of derivatives, including when the inner derivative is zero.

Forward difference D_f=(f(x+h)-f(x))/h uses x and x+h. If f is twice continuously differentiable nearby with |f''|≤M2, Taylor's remainder gives |D_f-f'(x)|≤M2*h/2 for h>0. For central D_c=(f(x+h)-f(x-h))/(2h), the equal even terms cancel; if f has a continuous third derivative with |f'''|≤M3, the two third-order remainders give|D_c-f'(x)|≤M3*h²/6. The O(h) and O(h²) claims require smoothness and all evaluation points in the domain.

blocks.source:
from fractions import Fraction

def cubic_differences(x,h):
    if any(type(v) not in (int,Fraction) or abs(v)>1000 for v in (x,h)) or h<=0:
        raise ValueError("expected bounded int/Fraction x and positive h")
    x,h = Fraction(x),Fraction(h)
    forward = ((x+h)**3-x**3)/h
    central = ((x+h)**3-(x-h)**3)/(2*h)
    return forward,central,3*x*x

for h in (Fraction(1,2),Fraction(1,4),Fraction(1,8)):
    forward,central,truth = cubic_differences(1,h)
    print(str(h),str(forward-truth),str(central-truth))
print(cubic_differences(0,Fraction(1,8))[1] == Fraction(1,64))
blocks.caption: Expected lines: 1/2 7/4 1/4; 1/4 13/16 1/16; 1/8 25/64 1/64; then True. For x³ the forward derivative error is 3xh+h² and central error is h² exactly. At x=1, halving h makes central truncation error one quarter; forward error approaches a one-half ratio. Exact Fraction arithmetic deliberately isolates truncation from floating evaluation error.

blocks.markdown: Let each function evaluation have absolute error at most η. Subtracting two evaluations can add errors: forward derivative perturbation is at most 2η/h; central perturbation is at most η/h. Combining with truncation gives bounds M2*h/2+2η/h and M3*h²/6+η/h. Smaller h reduces truncation but magnifies evaluation error. Balancing orders suggests h proportional to sqrt(η) for first-order and η^(1/3) for second-order methods, with scale/derivative constants included. These are model-dependent scales, not universal h values; η may include solver error, measurement noise and roundoff.

blocks.source:
# A deliberately unrepresentable increment on this binary float model.
x,h = 1.0,2.0**-60
print(x+h == x)
approximation = ((x+h)**2-x*x)/h
print(approximation)
print(2*x)
# A centered quotient at a kink can also look reassuring but be misleading.
for step in (0.5,0.125):
    centered = (abs(step)-abs(-step))/(2*step)
    right = (abs(step)-abs(0.0))/step
    left = (abs(-step)-abs(0.0))/(-step)
    print(centered,right,left)
blocks.caption: Expected output: True, 0.0, 2.0, then 0.0 1.0 -1.0 on each of two lines. On the recorded binary-float runtime, x+h equals x, so the nominal forward quotient is 0 despite derivative 2. At |x| with x=0, central differences return 0 at all steps, while right and left slopes disagree. Neither a tiny step nor a stable-looking central estimate proves derivative existence/accuracy.

blocks.markdown: Before a numerical derivative, state the function/domain and units, choose smooth interior or a justified one-sided boundary formula, compare several scale-appropriate representable steps, and compare with analytic/polynomial references where available. Check x+h≠x and x-h≠x, finite outputs, and an evaluation-error budget. A step sweep can reveal a plateau or inconsistency but is not an error certificate. Noisy/discontinuous stochastic programs may require a different estimand or estimator, not a smaller finite-difference step. Common random numbers change the error model and need their own treatment.

Independent transfer: expand both finite-difference formulas for f(x)=x² and explain why central difference is exact in exact arithmetic while forward error is h. Derive the slope-unit change between dollars and cents. Construct an asymmetric domain where a central step is invalid. Explain why |x| at 0 defeats a central-difference convergence check. Finally name the assumptions missing before claiming a derivative tolerance from a solver status.

References: [OpenStax derivative definition](https://openstax.org/books/calculus-volume-1/pages/3-1-defining-the-derivative), [FNC truncation/roundoff](https://fncbook.com/fd-converge/), and [evaluation-error analysis](https://aalexan3.math.ncsu.edu/articles/num_diff.pdf). Own examples separate exact polynomial truncation from a recorded floating collision. No generic differentiability or app-runtime certification follows from them.

summary: Derivatives are local, unit-bearing limits. Finite-difference order needs smoothness and domain validity; decreasing a step can worsen evaluation error or erase the increment, and a centered quotient can hide a kink.
